title: A researcher bought noreply.net. Companies started sending him secrets.
gist: Security researcher Cory Solovewicz owns noreply.us and noreply.net and has received over 437,000 automated emails containing other organizations' internal data, because companies send system mail to placeholder domains they wrongly assume nobody controls. A parallel effort by Xeal's Mike Sheward, who bought deleteduser.com for about $15 and got sensitive mail within the hour, shows the flaw is generic across the industry — the two have defensively bought 30+ domains, and Solovewicz's scan found 328 of 7,136 candidate placeholder domains already configured with catch-all inboxes.

insights.claim: Buying a domain that software treats as a null destination and enabling a catch-all inbox converts it into a passive data-exfiltration channel, because organizations send system-generated mail to placeholder addresses believing those messages go nowhere and cannot be monitored.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The attack requires only a domain registration and zero exploitation — the cheapest known route to bulk corporate data, and one no security budget currently covers.
insights.locator: After originally planning to use the noreply.us domain

insights.claim: A second and distinct failure mode is offboarding: rather than deleting accounts, companies rewrite a departing person's individual address to a placeholder domain, so mail intended for a former employee keeps flowing to whoever owns that domain.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Identity-lifecycle tooling is the root cause — an audit target for any company doing security due diligence on HR/IT integrations.
insights.quote: companies appear to be simply changing email addresses rather than entirely deleting accounts from their systems

insights.claim: The leaked traffic is entirely machine-generated — automated messages from company systems rather than human-written email — which means the exposure is continuous and unnoticed rather than the result of any single mistake.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Automated leakage does not self-correct; volume scales with the sender's transaction volume, so the biggest companies leak the most.
insights.quote: The messages are automated by company systems, not written by humans, the researcher says.
insights.locator: Overall, emails have been sent from more than 14,000

insights.claim: The problem is entirely avoidable with existing standards — companies could route system mail to internal domains or to the .invalid domain, which is guaranteed never to resolve.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A zero-cost fix exists, so continued exposure is a governance failure rather than a technical constraint — and therefore hard to defend in litigation.
insights.quote: companies could use internal domains or the .invalid domain that is guaranteed not to exist
insights.locator: While the issue is not a new one

insights.claim: One of Solovewicz's domains has registered 401,796 messages since December 2024, averaging 699.99 messages per day by his own calculation.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Seven hundred inadvertent corporate emails a day to a single accidental endpoint is the base rate for how leaky enterprise mail configuration actually is.
insights.quote: one of the domains at which the security researcher receives email has registered 401,796 messages—by his calculations that’s an average of 699.99 pings per day
insights.locator: Cory Solovewicz receives more unwanted emails than you

insights.claim: noreply.net has taken roughly 400,000 messages in eighteen months with 28,365 of them carrying attachments, while noreply.us received 37,255 messages across 2,345 days — a roughly tenfold higher per-day rate on the .net domain.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Nearly 30,000 attachments is the sharp end: documents, not just notifications, are the material breach exposure.
insights.locator: Solovewicz says that the noreply.net domain is the largest

insights.claim: The misdirected mail originates from more than 14,000 distinct 'from' addresses across 6,200 root domains, showing the misconfiguration is spread across thousands of independent organizations rather than concentrated in a few bad actors.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: 6,200 distinct sending organizations means this is an industry-wide default-configuration defect, likely inherited from shared SaaS and mail platforms.
insights.quote: emails have been sent from more than 14,000 “from” addresses, from 6,200 root domains
insights.locator: Overall, emails have been sent from more than 14,000

insights.claim: Solovewicz built a probe that scanned 7,136 candidate placeholder domains and found 328 already configured with catch-all inboxes, implying a substantial population of live collection points beyond the ones researchers control.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A 4.6 percent hit rate on untested placeholder domains suggests unknown parties are already harvesting this traffic at scale.
insights.quote: I’ve scanned 7,136 domains, and 328 of them were identified as having catch-all inboxes configured,
insights.locator: As part of his Defcon talk

insights.claim: Solovewicz explicitly frames his findings as a lower bound, saying what he accidentally found is likely the tip of the iceberg and declining to size the total problem.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Unbounded scope means any estimate of enterprise data-loss incidence based on disclosed breaches is materially understated.
insights.quote: my concern is that what I ‘accidentally’ found when I registered my domain is just the tip of the iceberg
insights.locator: As part of his Defcon talk

insights.claim: The leaked content spans injury reports from a city government, service and repair orders, school platform account setup emails, pizza order confirmations, and — most damagingly — large volumes of test platform credentials.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Credentials arriving unsolicited turn a passive leak into an active intrusion vector into the sending organization.
insights.quote: I get service orders for people that need repairs. I get lots of test platform credentials,
insights.locator: Over the last few years, he's received

insights.claim: Mike Sheward's domains have received emails from at least 100 different organizations including Viagra order confirmations, vacation and leave-of-absence approval requests, hotel bookings with full names, and Zoom invitations from a UK government agency.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Health-adjacent purchases and government meeting invitations are precisely the material for targeted extortion and social engineering.
insights.locator: Like Solovewicz, Sheward has seen thousands

insights.claim: One of the highest-volume senders to Sheward's domains is an AI company running object-recognition on workers at Middle East industrial sites to flag safety-protocol violations, which has sent him thousands of CCTV stills.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: AI surveillance vendors are piping raw biometric-adjacent imagery to unowned domains — a concrete near-term regulatory and reputational exposure for the computer-vision sector.
insights.quote: I am being a good guardian of the Internet dumpster—but if I had been a bad one, it’s not hard to see how this information that is willingly thrown at my face could be misused,
insights.locator: One of the most frequent sources of email

insights.claim: Sheward notes that cybersecurity companies and Microsoft partner companies are themselves among the senders leaking data to his placeholder domains.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Security vendors failing their own hygiene test undercuts the assumption that buying security software fixes configuration risk.
insights.quote: There’s a lot of cybersecurity companies and a few Microsoft partner companies as well,
insights.locator: Like Solovewicz, Sheward has seen thousands

insights.claim: Mike Sheward spent roughly $15 to acquire deleteduser.com and had sensitive email from three different organizations within the first hour of ownership.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Fifteen dollars and sixty minutes is the entire cost of entry — the economics guarantee adversaries are already doing this.
insights.quote: Within the first hour, there were three different organizations that had emailed stuff to @deleteduser.com,

insights.claim: Working independently, Solovewicz and Sheward have collectively purchased more than 30 placeholder domains specifically to deny them to malicious actors — an ad hoc, individually funded defense of a systemic internet weakness.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Critical exposure is being contained by two private individuals' credit cards; that is not a durable control and creates key-person risk for the whole ecosystem.
insights.locator: As both Solovewicz and Sheward realized

insights.claim: The failure is not novel — Brian Krebs documented companies sending millions of messages to @donotreply.com addresses nearly twenty years ago while at the Washington Post — meaning two decades of disclosure have failed to change enterprise defaults.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Twenty years of unfixed exposure argues awareness campaigns don't work here; only platform-level defaults or regulation will move it.
insights.quote: almost 20 years ago, independent security journalist Brian Krebs, then working at the Washington Post, wrote how companies were sending millions of messages to @donotreply.com emails
insights.locator: While the issue is not a new one

insights.claim: Notification results have been mixed: some organizations quietly fixed their configurations while many never replied, and the sheer number of affected senders makes individual notification impractical.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: When responsible disclosure cannot scale, the exposure persists by default — assume affected companies remain unaware and unremediated.
insights.locator: Both researchers say that, where possible

insights.claim: Solovewicz says handling every affected organization would now be a full-time job, and his Defcon talk is itself the responsible-disclosure mechanism because one-to-one notification has become impossible.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Public conference disclosure means adversaries now have the playbook at the same moment defenders do — expect copycat domain registrations immediately.
insights.quote: I’m at the point where this would now be a full-time job to handle every single one of these—that’s part of my motivation to talk about this, it is my responsible disclosure.

insights.claim: The core operating lesson is that no organization should assume a domain used as a mail sink is unmonitored, since ownership of any such domain can be bought by anyone at any time.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Any control that depends on 'nobody owns that domain' is one registration away from failing — an immediate audit item for mail and identity systems.
insights.quote: emphasizing that people shouldn’t assume a domain is unmonitored
